image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Two pie charts**.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Side-by-side panels**: the visualization places two separate pie charts next to each other.
- **No faceting grid or stacking** within charts.
- Categories are distinguished by **slice position** and **text labels/callouts**.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Survey question / topic (biggest problem vs agree/disagree statement) | Categorical/nominal | Separate chart/panel placement |
| Response category: Homelessness, War, Climate Change, Money, Other* | Categorical/nominal | Pie slice identity; external text labels/callouts |
| Percentage for biggest problem responses (42%, 31%, 17%, 6%, 4%) | Quantitative | Slice angle/area; numeric labels inside/near slices |
| Response category: Disagree, Agree, Don’t know | Categorical/nominal | Pie slice identity; external text labels/callouts |
| Percentage for agree/disagree responses (40%, 30%, 30%) | Quantitative | Slice angle/area; numeric labels inside slices |

comments.raw_comment: The pie charts are visually appealing and simple, but I don’t think they are the best way to compare the students’ answers. Some slices look very similar in size, which makes the differences hard to judge. A bar chart would have made the comparisons clearer. Still, the colours and layout make the chart easy to understand at a glance. The movie revenue chart looks cool because of the posters, but the design actually makes it harder to read the data. The images distract from the bar lengths, so it’s not easy to compare revenues across years. If I were to recreate it in Excel, I’d use a standard bar chart. I do like that the timeline is clear, but overall the chart focuses more on style than clarity.

comments.raw_comment:
1.  I notice that fourth graders often express their concerns about issues such as climate change, pollution, poverty, inequality, and conflicts. They may feel frustrated or worried about these problems and may not necessarily believe that adults are doing a good job of addressing them or running the world. They might perceive adults as not taking sufficient action or prioritizing short-term gains over long-term sustainability and well-being.

2. I wonder what fourth graders might think about various global challenges, such as environmental degradation, economic inequality, social injustice, and conflicts. They may question whether adults are effectively addressing these issues and making decisions in the best interest of future generations. They might also wonder about the role they can play in contributing to positive change and whether their voices will be heard and valued in discussions about the world's problems.

3. The results shown in the graphs and my opinion and my classmates might differ because I may not agree with the graph and my classmates may not agree because everyone has different perspectives on these types of topics.

4. "What wanders in a fourth graders mind and what wanders in a parents mind."

comments.raw_comment:
These paralleling graphs depict public opinion on major issues in the country and how people are handling those issues. The first graph asks what the major problems are with the answers including homelessness, war, money, climate change, and other. The second graph then elaborates on public sentiment on whether or no the older generations in power are handling these issues well. It can be inferred that the younger generations were the groups surveyed. Homelessness and the housing criss are prominent issues on the minds of Millennials and Gen Z. Similarly, climate change and current international issues are important to many young people and are prominent issues on social media. This inference is then furthered by the majority vote that Adults are not running the world well. It is unlikely for older people to vote against themselves, so it is fair to assume that the poll was held among younger people. This relates to me because I am a member of the younger generations. The results and my relationship to the graph make me wonder how my generation will run the country when it is our time. My generation is passionate and seems to be very discontented, so I am looking forward to seeing how these traits affect the future. 

“Our world, as run by adults”

I also notice that some of the problems that need solving are problems you wouldn't expect a young child to know/care about. It is also interesting that most of them feel adults are not doing a good job running the world. I wonder if this is just because they are children or because they genuinely have other reasons to disagree with the way the world is currently being run. I also wonder how their views will change as they grow up and if they will feel differently about their responses. This relates to me because these are real-world problems that I have thoughts and opinions on as well. I agree that these problems are some of the biggest issues that need fixing in today's world.

comments.raw_comment:
I noticed that 42% of people claimed that homelessness was the biggest problem that needed solving in the modern world. The second largest percentage of people (31%) says that war is the largest problem. The lowest percentage (4%) of people said that money was the largest problem. In the other pie chart, 30% agree that adults are doing a good job of running the world, and 40% disagree. The other remaining 30% claim they don’t know for sure.

I wonder why money is rated so lowly as a large problem, when it has ties to almost every other problem on the pie chart. I think it could be because it’s obvious that money is a problem, but people need to find a subject or problem caused by monetary issues that they could put a real name to. In this case, homelessness was chosen.

This shows me and others how large of a problem homelessness really is, and how many people disagree that the world is being run correctly. This is a reminder that the world, even though made more comfortable due to industrialization for many, still has massive imperfections and flaws that need to be addressed, such as homelessness and war.

comments.raw_comment: This graph is very interesting to me, I think it shows a lot of the pitfalls of humanity and our governmental systems right now. There are a lot of problems that need to be solved, and people are aware of them. However, not many people agree with the way that our government is being run and the people who are in control of it. People clearly have strong opinions and awareness regarding issues in the world that need to be solved. A lot of these issues are humanitarian, people are more worried about homelessness and war than economic issues like money. I think this shows how people feel, but it is not at all reflected in the actions of our society and government. I think this leads into the next graph and explains why people mostly do not agree with the state of the leaders and government of our country. Only 30% of people actually agree with the way things are, a number that is shockingly and worryingly low. I would title this graph: “How Successful is Our Society?”

comments.raw_comment:
1. Some things I noticed were that Fourth graders think that the main problems in the world are homelessness and war, which are indeed big problems. Still, there are only a few of them, compared to other things said, that think that money is the biggest problem, which surprises me how fourth graders know about war but don't know the struggles of money. I also noticed that more than half of them are unsure or don't think adults are doing a good job in the world. 
2. I wonder how the views of these children will change in a few years, I wonder if they would think the same or if they would have other things to say that are problems other than money or homelessness. I also wonder how many of their opinions on whether or not adults are doing a good job will change if they get asked again at the start of high school and the end of it if it would be more accurate to actual problems.
3. I can't entirely agree with half the results shown in the graph for the biggest problems that need to be solved, I do think that war is a major problem but I think Climate change should have bigger a percentage than 6 and I think other students would agree, Homelessness is definitely a big problem in LA but I don't think it's a major problem in the world like climate change or money. I agree with the graph about whether or not adults are doing a good job, I don't know if adults are, but I don't think they are doing the best they could be doing.
4. "What do fourth graders think adults suck at solving."

comments.raw_comment: This shows data from a survey asking fourth graders about big problems in the world, and if it's run the right way by adults. Those two topics can be put in the same category and have a lot in common as one of the problems in the world is the bad influence that many adults give off, which affects children. It can be this way for adults because of their childhood when older generations reflected negative habits on them. This caused the adults to get used to them and practice them because the adults in their background when they were young made it seem okay for bad acts to be committed. This rubs off on the youth as we see more cases of them beginning to do the same wrong things. For this reason, grown-ups must do a better job preaching good acts in kids' lives so bad habits won't get in the way of their future.

Thanks to all who responded.   Here are some of the catchy headlines posted:  “4th Grade Point of View: What’s Wrong With the World?” by Henry of Gull Lake High School in Richland, Mich.; “Little Kids with Big Opinions on Global Issues” by Michael of Mich.; two headlines from Traverse City West Senior High School in Mich. -- “Fourth Graders Take on World Issues. Are They More Aware Than You?” by Natalie and "Children Give Their Opinions On World Problems And How Well We're Doing” by Seth; "Kids Vote: What's Wrong With the World?" by Justin of Masterman School in Philadelphia and two headlines from Perth Amboy High School in N.J. -- "Kids Speak Up On World Problems" by Arturo and “Humanity's Problems: What Are the Kids Saying?” by Emily.

The next graph will be released by Friday, March 15 with live-moderation two weeks later on Wednesday, March 27.  The topic – Africa’s youth.
 
Signing off – Sharon Hessney from Boston, who has many questions she would ask students, such as “Which graph in this feature do you like the most and why?”, and DeAnna McDonald of Univ. of Arizona in Tucson, who was impressed that so many students recognized the difficulty in using these graphs to generalize to a population of all fourth graders.

comments.raw_comment:
This graph of what fourth graders think about the biggest issue that needs solving now is an interesting insight into what younger people think about our current situation. I noticed that the first pie chart's answers are related to current events. The most common issue that these fourth graders chose is homelessness. Currently, a lot of big states are being affected by homelessness. Some examples include  California(Skid Row, the Mole people, etc), New York, and many more states. The second most popular choice is war. As one may know, Russia is invading Ukraine. Though most of the attention has died down, it's still a big impact. The second chart asks about whether adults are doing a good job at running the world. Most fourth graders disagreed which I also agree with.

One thing I wonder about is whether these views are from a biased view of a fourth grader. These fourth graders might not fully view the world's current events, which might skew the results.

I feel that our class would have a drastically different answer. I feel that homelessness and war would be pushed down the list while other options would be pushed up. There would also be more of a consensus on whether the current adults are doing a good job at running the world.

One headline that fits this article is: "Fourth Graders - Can They Run A Country?"

comments.raw_comment: I notice that the responses given are inaccurate but align with what someone would imagine a 4th grader to answer. An example of this is homelessness being voted as the biggest problem that needs to be fixed. While it's not necessarily wrong, other large problems, such as world hunger, were voted what would seem disproportionately low. I think the reason that homelessness was voted so high was because of what the fourth graders experience in their everyday lives. The cities that the students that were interviewed come from, San Diego, Providence, and Spokane, are all cities with very high rates of homelessness. While it may be somewhat easy for a family to hide money problems or violence on the news from a kid, it's hard to hide homelessness. You can't just throw an invisibility cloak over people sleeping on stoops when you walk down the street. It is often hard for fourth graders to imagine other people's problems who live very different lives, so it may be hard for them to imagine war or the extreme hunger and lack of resources some people have to live with. comments.raw_comment:
Viewing the graph, I think it’s strange that 42% of these fourth graders think homelessness is the most serious issue in the present day. With so many other important issues on the world’s canvas, it’s interesting that nearly half decided on this. Similarly, 30% said war, rather than issues that could cause the entire world to face problems- such as climate change and world hunger. I definitely don’t oppose the two issues that the kids are so drawn to, but it’s definitely not what many adults and even teens would say. In the current world situation, I know that many Gen-Zers strongly oppose climate change, which I believe would hold the largest portion of the chart if they were the subjects.
        Additionally, I notice that a great portion of the students think adults are doing a poor job of running the world. It’s interesting that such young people have seemingly already opposed leaders of the world. That brings me to ask the question- Have adults taught them this? At the age they’re at, not many have access to news websites or social media, so all their knowledge of world leaders presumably comes from others. It’s quite strange!
	If it was up to me and my classmates, we’d surely have similar opinions about world leaders, but that comes from our knowledge of the world. However, I believe we’d definitely gravitate towards climate change rather than war and homelessness, as the kids voted.

In this graph, 4th graders are granted two questions. This first question is, "What is the biggest problem that needs solving right now?" and the second question is, "Do you agree or disagree with the statement: Adults are doing a good job of running the World." The answers to the first question were pretty basic or general saying things like homelessness, war, and climate change. I think these are expected responses, especially because I know I would've answered similarly when I was a 4th grader. What I thought was more interesting was the second graph. Young kids, especially at the age of a 4th grader, tend to be very honest. Seeing kids' feelings on such a broad question is important because they aren't trying to cover anything up.
         As a 7th grader, if kids in my class were asked these questions, I think the answers would be similar. Of course, the response to the first question might be a little more developed, but I think in general there would be similar opinions.

comments.raw_comment:
These two pie charts show 2 questions asked to four 4th-grade classrooms in Spokane Washington, Louisville Kentucky, Rhode Island, and San Diego California by the NYT.  The questions asked to these 4th graders were: the biggest problem that needs solving right now and do you agree or disagree with this statement that adults are doing a good job running the world? I noticed that the first question for the biggest problem that needs to be solved right now is that homelessness was the highest percentage at 42% and after that, the issue of war was rated at 31%. I noticed in the second pie chart that the kids disagreed that adults are doing a good job running the world at 40%. The kids were interviewed in large cities and said the major problem is homelessness makes sense because California is known to have a large homelessness problem. I wonder if the NYT interviewed kids in different smaller or more rural cities would homelessness be seen as a big problem in the world right now? Maybe a 4th-grader who lives in a more rural state would say that money or climate change is more important due to the large agricultural economy in that state. This relates to me and my community because I have traveled the country and have spent time in major cities that have a homelessness problem and have seen no change to fix the problem in these cities. 

Through the Eyes of a Fourth Grader

comments.raw_comment:
These two pie charts show how various groups of fourth graders across the US felt when asked political questions. The first question asked, “What is the biggest problem that needs solving right now?” showed a majority of fourth graders responded with either homelessness (42%) or war (31%). Other responses included climate change (17%) and money (4%). The second question “Do you agree or disagree: adults are doing a good job of running the world.” 40% of fourth-graders responded that they disagreed with the statement, 30% responded they agreed, and 30% responded they did not know. 

Students who were interviewed lived in places such as San Diego, Providence, and Spokane. All these cities have a huge homelessness problem. This makes sense as to why so many students voted homelessness as the biggest problem that needs solving. If the NYT interviewers had targeted other cities in the US, I wonder how these stats would change. I also wonder why so few children said that problems like bullying were the biggest since there has been a great increase in bullying throughout schools. Additionally, I noticed that, with the second question, the highest percentage of students said that they disagreed with the fact that adults are doing a good job running the world at 40%. I wonder what they are basing their answers off of such as if it’s from the news or just from what they witness in their communities everyday. I also wonder how these results would be different if the age of the children interviewed were different, such as maybe asking high school students instead. My headline for this graph would be: “The World Through the Lens of Fourth Graders”.

comments.raw_comment:
From the data, I noticed that the fourth graders polled voted homelessness as the biggest problem in the world at 42%. This was followed by war at 31%, and climate change at 17%. I find it interesting that the children voted climate change and war as larger issues in the world, because these problems could impact their generation the most as they grow up and become adults. The fourth graders also disagreed with the sentiment that adults are doing a good job of running the world. This makes me think that the children polled are fairly knowledgeable about world problems. I would have assumed that children would list bullying as a big world problem because that is something that is more likely to be addressed at that age. I also would have thought more children would think that adults were doing a good job in running the world by looking up to and relying on their own parents. I wonder how often fourth graders discuss the world problems listed in the pie chart in school or at home? How are they educated about these problems? I agree mostly with the children’s response to the biggest problems in the world that need to be solved. Personally, I would have listed homelessness, world hunger, war and climate change as large problems. My classmates probably would disagree with adults doing a good job running the world due to problems with climate change and war. 

“Should 4th-Graders Run the World?”

comments.raw_comment:
1. What do you notice? If your notice makes a claim, where in the graph is the evidence to support it?

This graph is a demonstration of what 4th graders think the world's biggest problems are along with if they think adults are doing a good job running the world. It is in pie chart format with two pie charts next to each other. Some of the biggest world problems mentioned include homelessness, climate change, war, and money. In the second chart about whether adults are doing a good job running the world the answers, I split into 30% yes, 30% I don't know, and 40% no. 

2. What do you wonder?

I wonder why so many kids said that homelessness was the world's biggest problem (42%) and why 40% seem to think that adults are not doing a good job running the world. I would assume that 4th graders think homelessness is such a significant issue because it's a problem they see often rather then rights issues for example. 

3. What impact does this have on you and your community?

I think it's important to see what our kids think the community's and world's biggest problems are to reflect on what we're focusing on. Moreover, I think it's a good self-reflection for adults to see if kids believe they are running the world well. 

4. What's going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea.

4th graders for congress

Are 4th graders better fit for leadership than adults?

I notice that fourth graders think that homelessness is the biggest problem currently that needs solving. I wonder if this is because homelessness is an issue that gets a decent amount of news coverage and one that many children may have experienced either in their hometowns or when traveling as it is so profound globally. I know that as a fourth grader, homelessness was definitely one of the issues that I had heard most about and one that I experienced living so close to N.Y.C. I also notice that 40% of fourth graders disagree with the statement that adults are doing a good job of running the world. This means that the majority of fourth graders believe adults are doing a good job of running the world. I wonder if this is because children are more likely to trust the adults in their community and look up to those older than them. As you get older it is likely your opinions will change as you gain new life experiences. Finally, I notice that only 4% of children think that money is a problem in the world that needs solving. I wonder if this is because many children do not comprehend many different aspects of finances and do not consider money as being an area of concern. I agree that homelessness is an incredibly significant issue in the world. However, I think that money is a much larger issue than it is depicted in the graph. Although inflation rates have decreased drastically since COVID-19, they have never reached the rates they were before. 

Fourth-grade Feelings!

Welcome to Wednesday's live moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  Today’s graphs are the results of student opinion surveys from fourth grade classes visited by New York Times journalists.  The students are from Spokane, Louisville, Providence and San Diego. 

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online for the four questions.  If your notice includes a claim, please back it up with evidence that supports your claim.  By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the free link to the online article that included these graphs, shout outs for some of the catchiest headlines and more.  

You can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

The next graph will be released by Friday, March 15, with live-moderation two weeks later on March 27.  The topic – Africa’s youth.

comments.raw_comment:
1) At first glance, I found it interesting that 42% of surveyed fourth graders perceived homelessness as the greatest threat and that 40% of surveyed fourth graders don’t believe the world is being run well by adults. Although homelessness is a disastrous problem that has to be dealt with, as a high schooler, I perceived war and climate change as much more alarming threats. This made me wonder why would a fourth grader be more concerned about homelessness than violence and worldwide disasters. I hypothesize that homelessness is a much easier threat to perceive. Whenever a fourth grader is out with his parents, he is unlikely to see war or the real-time effects of climate change. These are far away problems only heard of on TV, unlike homelessness, which he could see on the corner by his street. A fourth grader's concern over homelessness may add to the statistic that 40% of fourth graders do not find the world being run well.
Continuing my observation, I began to wonder how the survey was taken. If you look at the graphs, the survey was done on fourth graders in Spokane, Louisville, Providence, and San Diego which are all big cities. Homelessness is often most prevalent in big cities, where rent is higher and where there’s a greater concentration of people. If the survey was taken in rural America or deeper into the Suburbs, I wonder how the survey would change.

comments.raw_comment: I notice that most fourth graders believe homelessness is the biggest issue and that they don't believe adults are doing a good job of running the world. It was pretty shocking to me to see the things that these 9 to 10 year olds found problematic. I wonder the what extent these issues affect the children and how much they really care about these issues. I'm curious if the environment that they live in or the people in their lives have swayed their opinions or if they were formed on their own. I also wonder what might change about these charts if the survey was given to a larger demographic. I think the graphs are a pretty accurate representation of the mixed beliefs of my classmates, but I think these graphs show groups of issues rather than specific issues. For example, rather than saying the students in my school are worried about money, they may say that they're worried about inflation or the economy. My idea for a headline is "Step into the Mind of a 4th Grader: What is the World's Biggest Issue?"

comments.raw_comment: The graph on the left is about the biggest problems according to four fourth grade classrooms. Homelessness and war are the biggest problems, and I can definitely see why, considering those were some of the few problems I was aware of at that age. Also funny considering that the solutions to both of them are fairly easy. They are called: give people homes (make sure no suitable home is unoccupied for a long period of time), and not killing other people. The graph on the right is asking if adults are mismanaging the world. Most (40%) fourth graders believe that adults are not doing a good job of running the world. This relates to me because I definitely think adults are doing a horrible job running the world. I don't necessarily think children would do a better job, but some of the adults I talk to act like actual children, and yet they are the ones making major decisions.

comments.raw_comment:
It is a wide belief, even among fourth graders, that there are many things wrong with the world and not enough being done about it. According to the chart, homelessness and war are perceived as the most prominent global issues, and only 30% of fourth graders agree that adults are doing a good job running the world. Fourth graders are very perceptive and are in touch with the world around them; they are aware of the worldly issues and are worried that adults aren’t doing enough.
I wonder if the 4% of children worried about money and poverty experience it at home. I also wonder how much exposure (news as well as family conversations) these children get about worldly problems, and how censored it is. Are the problems they perceive as the biggest also the problems with closest proximity to them?
I think the graph is relatively accurate in my beliefs; I think there is quite a bit wrong in the world, and I believe there is more that can be done to solve those problems. It is not that I don’t think adults should be running the world, but I do believe there is a better way to manage the issues arising. I am surprised how small of a group is concerned about weapons considering the increase in school shootings recently. I wonder if this is due to parents shielding their children so they aren’t scared. 
"The Elementary Truth: Poverty, War, Climate Change - Are Adults Failing Us?"

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that there is a mention of bullying being one of the problems the world needs to solve. As a student, I think that bullying is not really in the top 8 of the world’s problems, but it is likely important to fourth graders. I also notice that nearly half of the students thought that adults weren’t running the world well. This is probably because children are rebellious and don’t realize that their ideas or plans wouldn't work in the real world.

What do you wonder?
I wonder if the data would differ if it was taken in different states in the country. Places like Hawaii, Alaska, Texas, etc. I also wonder how the children’s views shift as they get older, possibly shifting away from bullying being an issue. Along those lines, I also wonder about the change in the children’s trust in adults. I think it would be higher in younger grades like kindergarten or 1st, dip down, then go back up again in middle school and high school.

How do the results shown in the graphs differ from your opinion and that of your classmates?
The results differ because high schoolers certainly have a different worldview than 4th graders. For example, bullying is not at the forefront of my mind. Additionally, I think adults are doing the best they can to run the world; I would not likely do better.

I also wonder how the results would differ if the children were older because I know that my personal views on the world have changed quite a bit from when I was younger. 
Difference:

I also think that our parents are more open to us about the issues in the world and their opinions, so that may also affect our opinions more than when we were fourth graders. I also think everyone has a different perspective because everyone has different relations to certain problems which could make us more passionate about a specific issue.

What do you notice?
I noticed that 40% of the fourth graders believed that adults are not doing a good job running the world. If it is so blatant that even fourth graders can see that our world is not being run well, then why is it not spoken about more? I also noticed how homelessness and war seemed to be the biggest problems in the world to them. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder if the first pie chart would differ in different parts of the country. I wonder if the location of the students will affect what they believe to be the biggest problems, or if the political parties of their parents have a heavier influence on their thoughts. 

How do the results shown in the graphs differ from your opinion and that of your classmates?
Although only 17% of the students thought climate change was the biggest issue, I believe that it is a bit more important than that. Although climate change may not be more important than homelessness or war, it is still a huge issue that needs to be spoken about more publicly; because unlike some of the other issues brought up, it is irreversible. We must globally achieve net-zero carbon emissions no later than 2050 in order to avoid the harmful effects of global warming.

comments.raw_comment: As many older siblings and parents know, 4th graders are normally pretty sincere and honest about the things that they talk about. This can be seen in the data pulled from the graph. Many of the children find that homelessness and war are the main problems affecting us, with climate change trailing behind. This outlook on life comes from kids who normally lead simple easy lives without a lot of complications, so when they think something is a problem, it is a major problem. Most of them also believed that the adults were not leading the world properly. If we have a younger generation telling us that we have problems then we should work to change those things. They notice what we can’t and because of this they sometimes are more aware and wary of the problems that they see. The problems that they notice in the world are some of the same problems that my friends and I notice in the world around us. In surrounding areas where I live, there are large  populations of homeless people and it  is not uncommon to find many of them camping along the roadside. Being  near the ocean also allows us to notice the effects of climate change as  the summers have become hotter and the winters colder than they have ever been. In the past two years alone there  have been hail storms that haven’t happened previously for an incredibly long time. All in all, I think that it is a smart decision to listen to and support the thoughts of these fourth graders.

comments.raw_comment:
After looking at the graph I noticed most kids agree adults are doing a bad job of running the world, and the biggest problem that needs solving is Homelessness. The rest are unsure or agree that they are running the world well. I also noticed a majority believe that Homelessness and war are the biggest issue, while the other issues are distributed evenly but very few think money or climate change is the issue.

I wonder where this survey was held as some countries or places have different problems than others, and if they think adults are doing a bad job because of parents not letting them do what they want or taking care of their families poorly, and if their parents can play a part in their beliefs as sometimes they can blurt out a problem going on which influences the 4th grader. I also wonder if they think Homelessness is the biggest problem for them because that is what they can see in the city or outside of their homes compared to money and climate change problems since they do not experience it directly in front of their eyes. 

The results differ as my classmates and I have more of an understanding of what goes on in the real world compared to 4th graders. Because of this, there were different perspectives resulting in more people not agreeing with adults running the world well. A headline that could capture the graph’s main idea is “An Inside of the 4th grader’s View on the World”.

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that 4th graders think the biggest problem that needs solving is homelessness. Aside from just homelessness, these fourth graders also have a pretty broad spectrum of the issues that they identified, and all of these issues are big problems in our world right now. I also notice that they generally don't believe that adults are doing a great job of running the world.

I wonder how much of the information is based on their parents, and how the political party of their parents relates to their perspective on these issues. I also wonder how much of their perspective is based solely on what they can see, possibly contributing to why homelessness is identified as such a big issue. (For example, since kids are able to see homelessness more often in the world around them, it could make the issue feel more real.)

This relates to our community because there are many kids in our area, so it's very interesting to see what they think are big issues and how these may worry them since the graph shows they're concerned that the adults in the world aren't doing a good enough job of confronting and solving these issues. I don't know if it's a good thing that on the one hand kids have the awareness to identify big issues in their community, but on the other hand these fourth graders should just be kids, and not have to worry about these big issues and be able to so accurately pinpoint these issues.

A possible headline could be "Are You Smarter Than a 4th Grader: World Issues Edition"

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that  according to 4th graders, the biggest problem that needs solving right now is homelessness, and 40 out of 100% disagree with the statement that adults do a good job of running the world.
What do you wonder?
I wonder if their answers are influenced by what they are learning in school and the options that the teacher may have given them. Because they are only 4th graders, I wonder if some of their answers are solely based on their opinion instead of their knowledge. As an example, most kids like being in charge and if they had the chance to do so, they would because they would think they would have the freedom to do whatever they wanted instead of being told "no" by their parents.
How do the results shown in the graphs differ from your opinion and that of your classmates?
They differ from me and my classmates because we are more educated than 4th graders and we understand the responsibilities of being in charge or being a leader. Because of this, there would probably be a larger percent in 'war' on the left graph, and based on the opinions of my classmates for the right graph, there would most likely be a higher percent in 'agree.'

"Do Fourth Graders Actually Understand Our World's Biggest Issues?"

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that the fourth graders believe homelessness, war, and climate change are the biggest problems. I am surprised that they knew enough about these topics to know they are a problem. I was also surprised that only 30% of fourth graders believe adults are good at running the world. Maybe they didn't take the poll seriously, but these fourth graders seem much more observant than most people would believe. 

I wonder what type of education/new exposure these kids are open to, and how much it influenced their position. I wonder how the fourth graders determine whether something is more/less important than something else. I wonder how these fourth-grade answers would compare to those of a first-grader, a high school student, and the average adult.

Me and many people in my class would agree with the fourth graders, that adults are not doing a great job at running the world. Maybe we are biased because we are not adults, or maybe we blame the adults in charge for all the bad things that happen. Personally, I don't think all adults do a bad job, but I think we could be doing much better. I would agree that homelessness and war are top issues and that climate change is a major up-and-coming problem. I would show more concern for the economy and weapons (at least in America), as well as mental health issues in younger generations. 

Catchy Headline -->
A Look Inside a Fourth Grader's Mind: What's Wrong In Their World?

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that most fourth graders think that homelessness (42%) and war (31%) are the biggest problems that need solving. I also notice that climate change (17%) and money (4%) are far less prevalent. Many fourth graders disagree (40%) that adults are running the world well.

I wonder why so many fourth graders think homelessness is the biggest issue facing the world. Perhaps it is because they see unhoused people on the street, which presents a more obvious issue than climate change. I also wonder why war is considered the second biggest problem-- it would be helpful to know when the data was collected (ex. when the Russo-Ukrainian War or Israel–Hamas war began). I wonder how the internet has changed fourth graders' perceptions. Perhaps the news has caused them to believe adults are doing a poor job.

I think that climate change, war, and world hunger are the biggest problems that need solving. My classmates think homelessness is the largest issue, displacing climate change in importance. This relates to me and my community because young people will soon be able to vote and have their voices addressed. When today's youth "run" the world, my hope is that more people will agree that adults are doing a good job of it. I think that adults are doing a fine job, but need to lessen their polarization.

comments.raw_comment:
I think kids are more perceptive than we give them credit for. Clearly they can tell that the state of our country needs work. I think America needs to get its priorities straight and only then we’ll be able to come together.

As for the biggest issues our world faces today. I would accredit homelessness being on the top of the list to the proximity kids have to the issue. At least for kids living in the U.S. war is not close to home, but the people you see sleeping on the street on the way to school are.
